neighbours.label: the name of a packaged snack, candy or toy brand in a consumer/snacking context (Doritos, Skittles, Oreos, Legos), on its first piece, as opposed to the same sentences without a branded snack being consumed
fire: During the movie, my brother finished a whole tube of Pringles.
She packed a sleeve of Oreos for the long drive.
The vending machine only had Cheetos and Snickers left.
We bribed the kids with a bowl of Froot Loops to get them dressed.
He stocked the dorm fridge with Fritos and cans of soda.
The children built a castle out of Lego bricks all afternoon.
Grandma always kept a jar of Tootsie Rolls by the door.
At the party, someone spilled a bag of Funyuns on the rug.
quiet: During the movie, my brother fell asleep on the sofa.
She packed a spare jacket for the long drive.
The ticket machine only took coins and small notes.
We bribed the kids with an extra story to get them dressed.
He stocked the dorm shelves with textbooks and notebooks.
The children built a castle out of cardboard boxes all afternoon.
Grandma always kept a spare key by the door.
At the party, someone spilled red paint on the rug.

predictions: branded snack names 0.6-0.85; matched sentences with no snacking and no brand below 0.2
notes: Card: peaks on first pieces of brand names (' Sk'oal, ' Sk'ittles, ' Dor'itos, ' Tw'inkies, ' Cheer'ios, ' Leg'os, ' M'&M's); suppresses cereal/juice/candy/soda. Probe: Doritos 0.814, Skittles 0.830, Legos 0.803, Cheerios 0.675, Twinkies 0.665; 'eating a giant bag of carrots' 0.609 (peak ' eating', the snacking setup alone fires), 'packs of batteries' 0.288, Toyota 0.001. Near misses remove both brand and snacking setup.
